## Example

Take $n = 1$ and define
$$T:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R},\qquad T(x) = -x.$$

$T$ is linear and invertible (its inverse is itself).

## Proof that no $S$ with $e^S = T$ exists

Suppose, for contradiction, that there exists a linear transformation $S:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ with $e^S = T$.

Every linear map $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is multiplication by a unique real number. So $S$ is multiplication by some $s\in\mathbb{R}$, and $T$ is multiplication by $-1$.

The matrix exponential of a $1\times 1$ matrix $[s]$ is
$$e^S = e^{[s]} = [e^s].$$

Thus $e^S = T$ becomes
$$e^s = -1.$$

But the real exponential function satisfies $e^s > 0$ for every $s\in\mathbb{R}$. This contradicts $e^s = -1 < 0$.

Hence no real linear transformation $S:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfies $e^S = T$.

## Conclusion

The transformation
$$\boxed{T(x) = -x \text{ on } \mathbb{R}^1}$$
is invertible yet admits no real logarithm, i.e. there is no linear $S:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ with $e^S = T$.

*(The underlying reason: a real invertible matrix has a real logarithm iff each Jordan block size for each negative real eigenvalue occurs an even number of times. The $1\times 1$ matrix $[-1]$ has a single Jordan block of size $1$ for the negative eigenvalue $-1$ — an odd count — so no real logarithm exists.)*

### PROOF COMPLETE
thinking:
The problem asks for an invertible linear transformation T: R^n → R^n such that there is no linear transformation S with e^S = T.

Key fact: A real matrix has a real logarithm (i.e., is e^S for some real matrix S) if and only if... the condition is about Jordan blocks for negative eigenvalues. Specifically, a real invertible matrix A has a real logarithm if and only if each Jordan block corresponding to a negative eigenvalue occurs an even number of times (for each size).

So a simple example: T = -I on R^1 (n=1). Then T = -1. Is there a real S with e^S = -1? e^S for real S is positive. So no. But wait, -I on R^1 is just the scalar -1, e^S = -1 has no real solution since e^s > 0 for real s. So T(x) = -x on R^1 works.

But let me double check the condition. Actually for n=1, T = -1 (scalar). e^S = -1 needs real S (1x1 matrix, i.e., real number s). e^s = -1 impossible. So T: R → R, T(x) = -x is invertible and has no real logarithm.

That's the simplest example. Let me write the proof.

Actually, let me reconsider — the problem says R^n, n could be anything ≥ 1. n=1 is fine.

Proof: Take n=1, T: R → R defined by T(x) = -x. This is invertible. Suppose there exists a linear S: R → R with e^S = T. A linear map R → R is multiplication by some real number s. Then e^S is multiplication by e^s. So e^s = -1. But e^s > 0 for all real s, contradiction. Hence no such S exists.

### PROOF COMPLETE
